newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Plans for world criminal court held up by haggling.
newsitem.headline: Plans for world criminal court held up by haggling.

text.p: Plans to set up a permanent international criminal court have been held up by haggling over just how independent it should be, experts and academics said.

As the ad-hoc tribunals dealing with grave breaches of human rights in former Yugoslavia and Rwanda press ahead with their work, efforts to create a permanent successor to them are still bogged down with preliminaries.

"The major powers...are not ready to move at this stage towards the establishment of such a court. They all feel that it is premature and that it needs more time to mature politically," said Professor Cherif Bassiouni of DePaul University in Chicago.
Bassiouni is vice-chairman of a U.N. committee set up to draft a statute for a permanent court to try individuals suspected of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
This preparatory committee has held two three-week sessions this year but Bassiouni said it had made little headway on core issues because some countries were bent on delaying the project.
One big problem has been the relationship between the court and the powerful U.N. Security Council where Britain, China, France, Russia and the U.S. have permanent seats and a veto.
"The United States, the United Kingdom and France would like to have a court, but they would like to see it under the control of the Security Council," said Bassiouni.
"Then you have a core group of about 50 countries, mostly Europeans...who want a truly independent court."
Bassiouni, speaking in a personal capacity, said the battle centred on whether the Security Council or an independent prosecutor would play the key role in launching prosecutions.
He said he favoured complete independence of the proposed court from the Security Council, arguing that this would bring it into line with universally accepted principles of government.
"Everybody now recognises that the judiciary...should be independent of the political branch of government," he said.
Professor Adam Roberts of Oxford University said U.N. members would remain wary of setting up a permanent criminal court until they could examine the small print.

"For example will Russia support an international criminal court if it might issue warrants against Russian officers involved in Chechnya? All states have skeletons in the cupboard that will make them nervous," he said.

Roberts, editor of "Documents on the Laws of War", said the debate over who controls the process of prosecution made it unlikely that a permanent court would be set up soon: "I'm not particularly optimistic. I think it will take time."
He said it was more likely that the ad-hoc tribunal in The Hague would undergo gradual expansion of its responsibilities to include crises occurring in other regions of the world.
Bassiouni believes that a permanent court will eventually be established, though initially at least it might not be as independent and powerful as he would have hoped.
"I think it will probably be watered down, that's my fear... but it can be amended subsequently and we can enhance it."
Bassiouni said the limited success of the Yugoslav and Rwanda tribunals in getting suspects into the dock had not reduced public support for international criminal prosecutions.
"People see that as a political impediment. They don't see it as an inherent weakness. I think that world public opinion is able to separate the wheat from the chaff," he said.
Roberts said the two ad-hoc tribunals had inevitably run into problems as they were borne out of the Security Council's reluctance to take decisive action in Bosnia and Rwanda.
"They were something of a substitute for action...It's a classic problem of political theory that law without power is rather weak law and that's what we see with these tribunals."
The U.N. General Assembly is due to review the project for a permanent criminal court in late October.
Bassiouni hopes it will ask the preparatory committee to finish its work by April 1, 1998 so a diplomatic conference can be called to finalise the text of a treaty setting up the court.
Nick Howen, head of legal affairs for London-based human rights group Amnesty International, urged U.N. members to press ahead and set up the court.
"The future of this court really hangs in the balance now. The 185 member states of the United Nations...have the power to make this court a reality," he said.
